article.title: U.S. Complicity Shaped a Catastrophe
article.author: Rick Chertoff, Dick Price, Robert Corsini
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Israeli assault on Gaza cannot be understood by beginning the story on October 7, 2023. That was one of the central arguments advanced during a panel titled “The Gaza Genocide” at the fourth annual Left Coast Forum, held October 2–4, 2026, at California State University, Los Angeles. Featuring longtime Jewish peace activist Rick Chertoff and historian Dr. Mahmood Ibrahim, the discussion challenged familiar narratives about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and examined the history of dispossession, occupation, failed diplomatic initiatives, and American military support that preceded the current catastrophe. The panel also confronted a question that has become increasingly urgent: What will it take to end the destruction of Gaza and establish a future in which Palestinians and Israelis can live with equal rights and security? The Gaza Genocide (23:10) The Conflict Did Not Begin With Hamas One of the panel's central arguments was that Israel's conflict with Palestinians long predates the establishment of Hamas in 1987. “There was no Hamas in 1948,” one panelist emphasized, referring to the year Israel was established and hundreds of thousands of Palestinians were displaced during what Palestinians call the Nakba, or catastrophe. Nor did Hamas exist during the 1967 war, when Israel occupied the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem. This history, the speakers argued, undermines explanations that present Hamas as the fundamental cause of Palestinian suffering. Ibrahim traced the organization's emergence to political developments during the 1980s, including the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood, the first Palestinian intifada, and widespread frustration with the inability of secular Palestinian organizations to achieve liberation. He challenged the simplified claim that Israel created Hamas. Instead, he argued, Israeli authorities recognized opportunities to exploit divisions between religious and secular Palestinian movements, weakening the possibility of a unified Palestinian political response. Those divisions would eventually become central to the breakdown of efforts to achieve Palestinian self-determination. Related: The Erasure of Palestine Gaza and the Failure of the Peace Process The panel examined Israel's 2005 withdrawal of approximately 8,000 settlers from Gaza and the subsequent deterioration of conditions in the territory. Although the withdrawal removed Israeli settlements from Gaza, it did not establish Palestinian sovereignty. Israel retained extensive control over Gaza's borders, airspace, and maritime access, while Egypt also controlled access through its border. After Hamas won the 2006 Palestinian legislative elections and subsequently consolidated control over Gaza, Israel intensified restrictions on the territory. The panelists described the repeated Israeli military assaults that followed as part of a continuing strategy of containment and destruction rather than a genuine effort to resolve the underlying conflict. They referred to the Israeli military expression “mowing the lawn,” used by some Israeli security strategists to describe recurring operations intended to degrade Palestinian armed groups' capabilities. For the speakers, that expression illustrated the normalization of periodic military violence against an already confined population. They also recalled the Great March of Return demonstrations in 2018 and 2019, when Palestinians gathered near Gaza's perimeter fence demanding the right of return and an end to the blockade. Israeli forces killed more than 200 Palestinians and injured thousands during those protests, according to United Nations reporting. The panelists argued that these events, together with expanding Israeli settlement activity, violence in the West Bank, and diplomatic initiatives that marginalized Palestinian demands, formed an essential backdrop to October 7. Understanding that history, they maintained, is necessary without excusing attacks on civilians. Related: J.D.’s Rant to Israel: “Wake Up and Smell the Reality!” The American Role: Weapons, Money, and Political Protection A particularly forceful exchange emerged when an audience member challenged the effectiveness of continued discussion while Palestinians were being killed. The participant demanded that the United States stop supplying Israel with weapons and financial assistance, insisting that verbal condemnations were insufficient. The speakers largely agreed with the urgency of that demand. Chertoff emphasized that political change rarely happens immediately. Drawing on his experience with social movements, he compared the struggle to end American support for Israel's military operations with the long campaign against the Vietnam War. Mass movements, he argued, often require years of organizing before they can force political leaders to change course. Yet he also suggested that public opposition to American policy toward Israel has developed far more rapidly than opposition to the Vietnam War did. The discussion highlighted campaigns to block weapons shipments, pressure Congress, support the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, and elect candidates willing to challenge unconditional military assistance to Israel. The speakers also criticized the role of political messaging in maintaining support for the assault on Gaza, arguing that misleading and inflammatory claims have helped justify continued military operations. For the panelists, exposing those narratives is inseparable from the work of building an effective movement for Palestinian rights. Is a Two-State Solution Still Possible? The discussion concluded with a question about the political future of Israel and Palestine. Asked whether he supported a two-state solution, Chertoff answered unequivocally that he did not. His objection was not simply ideological. He argued that the fragmented territories envisioned for a Palestinian state would lack the geographical continuity, economic independence, and freedom of movement necessary for meaningful sovereignty. He described the Palestinian state imagined under the Oslo framework as effectively a “telephone booth with a flag.” A territory whose borders, trade, transportation, and access to the outside world can be controlled by another government, he suggested, cannot function as a genuinely independent nation. But Chertoff did not offer a rigid alternative blueprint. Instead, he argued that Palestinians and Israelis must ultimately determine their own political arrangements, whether through a single democratic state, a confederation, or another structure. What matters, he maintained, is ending coercive domination and creating conditions in which people can negotiate their future as equals. The panel also acknowledged the challenge posed by divisions within Palestinian political leadership and the absence of a unified strategy for liberation. Yet the speakers suggested that demanding a comprehensive political program from a population experiencing massive destruction overlooks the conditions under which Palestinians are struggling to survive. Related: The Mamdani Win and the Losing Ethos of the Democratic Party From Outrage to Organized Political Power The discussion's most important conclusion was that the future of Gaza cannot be separated from American political choices. The United States is not merely an outside observer. Through military assistance, diplomatic protection, and its influence over regional politics, Washington possesses enormous power to shape events. The panelists argued that Americans who oppose the destruction of Gaza must therefore move beyond expressions of outrage toward sustained political organization capable of changing U.S. policy. The struggle, as they described it, is not simply about securing a ceasefire or negotiating another temporary arrangement. It is about confronting the structures of military domination, dispossession, and unequal rights that have defined Palestinian life for generations. The question left hanging over the room was whether Americans can build a movement strong enough to force their government to stop enabling those structures. For Chertoff and Ibrahim, the answer depends less on another round of diplomatic promises than on the willingness of ordinary people to organize, exert pressure, and demand a fundamentally different relationship between the United States, Israel, and Palestine.
